findings.quote: A particle's speed is proportional to cos of its phase.
findings.note: The particle velocity ∂y/∂t = −0.4 cos(kx − ωt) is proportional to the cosine; the speed is the magnitude of that, so it is proportional to |cos|. This question turns on exactly the speed-versus-velocity distinction, and the sentence as printed erases it — read literally it would force equal cosines and give Δx = λ, contradicting the same step's own conclusion that a phase gap of π also works.
findings.fix: A particle's velocity is proportional to the cosine of its phase, and its speed is the magnitude of that velocity.

notes: My own solve: k = 5π rad m⁻¹ so λ = 2π/5π = 0.4 m. Particle velocity is −0.4 cos(kx − ωt); two particles keep equal speed at every instant only when |cos(kx₁ − ωt)| = |cos(kx₂ − ωt)| for all t, which requires kΔx = nπ. The smallest non-zero separation is Δx = π/k = 0.2 m = λ/2 — option 4, the solution's answer. I confirmed numerically that Δx = 0.2 m and 0.4 m hold equal speed at all sampled times while Δx = 0.1 m does not. The remaining equations and the why_this_step (velocities exact negatives, speeds equal) are correct, and the common_mistakes entry correctly identifies 0.4 m as the separation for identical velocity. Difficulty 'hard' is defensible for this paper.
